blocks.text: A complete eye examination is a systematic assessment of visual function, the external eye, ocular movements, pupillary responses, the anterior segment, and the posterior segment. In clinical practice and OSCEs, you should be able to perform each step correctly, explain what you are testing, identify abnormal findings, interpret their significance, and present your findings clearly.

The examination is especially important for detecting refractive errors, cataracts, glaucoma, retinal disease, optic nerve disorders, cranial nerve palsies, and neurological lesions affecting the visual pathway.
Snellen chart or an equivalent logMAR chart, with appropriate distance and near-vision charts.
For external inspection, pupil assessment, and checking the corneal light reflex.
For red reflex assessment and fundoscopy.
For screening common red–green colour vision deficiencies.

items: Slit lamp and other equipment, if available

blocks.text: For detailed anterior-segment examination; an intraocular pressure device may also be needed.
Other useful equipment includes an occluder, a near-vision card, a fixation target, a ruler or measuring scale, and a fluorescein strip when indicated.
Wash your hands and introduce yourself.
Confirm the patient's identity and explain the examination.
Obtain consent and ask about pain, photophobia, and current visual symptoms.
Ensure adequate lighting, with the ability to dim the room for fundoscopy.
Ask whether the patient normally wears glasses or contact lenses.
Assess each eye separately, then compare both eyes together where appropriate.

Important: Ask about the onset and duration of visual symptoms, whether one or both eyes are affected, and whether the problem is painful or painless. Sudden visual loss, a painful red eye with reduced vision, a new curtain-like shadow, or new flashes and floaters require urgent assessment.
Before testing individual functions, inspect the patient from the front and, if necessary, from the side.

content_groups.group_title: A. Facial symmetry and orbital appearance

blocks.text: Look for:
Facial asymmetry.
Abnormal head posture or a compensatory head tilt.
Proptosis (forward displacement of the globe).
Enophthalmos (posterior displacement of the globe).
Periorbital swelling, bruising, or erythema.
Abnormal position of the eyes, including strabismus.
Facial scars, skin lesions, or signs of previous trauma.
Proptosis may occur in thyroid eye disease, orbital tumours, inflammation, or orbital haemorrhage.
Enophthalmos may occur after orbital trauma or with certain orbital disorders.
A head tilt may be a compensation for diplopia, including that associated with a fourth cranial nerve palsy.
Inspect for:
Ptosis: drooping of the upper eyelid.
Ectropion: outward turning of the eyelid.
Entropion: inward turning of the eyelid.
Blepharitis: inflammation of the eyelid margins.
Styes or chalazia.
Lid retraction, crusting, lesions, and abnormal eyelashes.
Incomplete eyelid closure, which may expose the cornea.

Ptosis may result from levator muscle dysfunction, oculomotor nerve palsy, or Horner syndrome. Acute ptosis accompanied by a dilated pupil or ophthalmoplegia is particularly concerning for a neurological emergency.
Inspect the conjunctiva by gently asking the patient to look up and down.
Look for:
Conjunctival injection or redness.
Pallor of the conjunctiva.
Discharge, chemosis (conjunctival oedema), or follicles.
Scleral icterus.
Corneal opacity, scars, or an irregular surface.
A visible foreign body or abnormal corneal appearance.
Do not press on a potentially injured eye. If an open-globe injury is suspected, avoid manipulating the eye or measuring intraocular pressure.
Look for excessive tearing, discharge, and swelling around the lacrimal sac near the medial canthus. Painful swelling in this region may indicate dacryocystitis.
Visual acuity is the ability to distinguish fine detail. It is one of the most important measurements in the eye examination and should usually be assessed early.
Equipment: Snellen chart, appropriate lighting, occluder, and the patient's usual distance glasses if applicable.
Position the patient at the distance specified for the chart, conventionally 6 metres.
Ensure the chart is correctly illuminated.
Ask the patient to wear their usual distance spectacles if normally required.
Cover the left eye without applying pressure.
Ask the patient to read the smallest line they can identify reliably.
Record the result for the right eye.
Repeat with the right eye covered to assess the left eye.
Test both eyes together if appropriate.
If acuity is reduced, repeat with a pinhole, if available.
Test each eye independently because one eye may have reduced vision despite apparently normal binocular vision.
Visual acuity is commonly recorded as a fraction:
(d): testing distance.
(D): distance at which a person with standard vision would read the same line.
For example, a patient with 6/18 vision sees at 6 metres what a person with standard acuity can see at 18 metres.
These values are examples, not a complete grading system for every cause of visual impairment. The correct interpretation depends on the testing method, the eye tested, and the clinical context.

content_groups.group_title: C. What if the patient cannot read the chart?

blocks.text: Proceed systematically using the chart and local protocol:
Pinhole acuity: If vision improves, a refractive error is likely contributing.
Counting fingers (CF): Ask the patient to count fingers at a specified distance.
Hand movements (HM): Ask whether the patient can detect hand movement.
Perception of light (PL): Determine whether the patient can detect a light source.
Projection of light: If light is perceived, assess whether its direction can be identified.
No perception of light (NPL): No light is perceived.

Record the actual test and distance, for example, right eye: counting fingers at 1 metre. These methods are not interchangeable, and severely reduced vision requires urgent evaluation when new or unexplained.
A pinhole occluder allows only central rays of light to enter the eye, reducing the blur caused by many refractive errors.
Interpretation:
Improvement suggests that refractive error is contributing to reduced acuity.
Little or no improvement raises concern for other causes, including cataract, corneal opacity, macular disease, or optic nerve pathology.
The pinhole test is a screening aid, not a definitive diagnosis. Severe refractive errors and other conditions may complicate interpretation.
Use a near-vision card at its specified testing distance, commonly around 35–40 cm.
Test each eye separately.
Ensure the patient uses appropriate near spectacles where applicable.
Record the smallest print read reliably.
Reduced near vision may occur with presbyopia, uncorrected refractive errors, macular disease, or other ocular disorders.
OSCE exam tip: Never write simply “vision normal.” Record the measured acuity in each eye, whether correction was used, and the result of pinhole testing if performed.
Visual fields assess the area of space visible to a person when their gaze is fixed on one point.
They help detect lesions involving the retina, optic nerve, optic chiasm, optic tract, optic radiations, or occipital cortex.
Sit opposite the patient at approximately arm's length.
Ask the patient to cover one eye and fix their gaze on your corresponding open eye.
Test the other eye similarly.
Extend your arms into the patient's peripheral visual field.
Present one or more fingers, or use a small target, moving from the periphery towards the centre.
Ask the patient to indicate when the target is first seen.
Compare their field with your own, assuming your visual fields are normal.
Test the superior, inferior, nasal and temporal regions.
Repeat for the other eye.
If indicated, test central vision using a fixation target and assess for central scotomas.
You can also compare simultaneous stimuli in both temporal fields to screen for a gross temporal field defect.
Important: Confrontation testing is a screening method. Subtle visual field defects require formal perimetry.

content_groups.group_title: B. Visual field abnormalities and their significance

blocks.text: A central area of reduced vision. It may occur in macular disease or optic neuropathy.
Loss of the temporal half of the visual field in both eyes. Classically associated with optic chiasm compression, such as from a pituitary mass.
Loss of the same side of the visual field in both eyes. A right homonymous defect generally indicates a lesion of the left retrochiasmal visual pathway, and vice versa.
Loss of the upper or lower half of the field. It can occur with retinal or optic nerve disease, including ischaemic optic neuropathy.
Other patterns include arcuate scotomas and nasal steps, which may occur in glaucoma.

content_groups.group_title: C. Localising a visual pathway lesion

blocks.text: A useful anatomical sequence is:
Retina and optic nerve: defects may be monocular.
Optic chiasm: classically produces bitemporal field loss.
Optic tract, optic radiations and occipital cortex: produce contralateral homonymous defects.
A lesion of the left optic tract, for example, causes a right homonymous visual field defect.
Exam clue: A patient with headache, endocrine symptoms and loss of peripheral vision on both temporal sides may have a compressive lesion near the optic chiasm.
Pupillary assessment evaluates the autonomic pathways controlling pupil size and helps identify optic nerve and oculomotor abnormalities.

content_groups.group_title: A. Inspect pupil size and shape

blocks.text: Observe both pupils before shining a light.
Assess:
Size in bright and dim lighting.
Symmetry.
Shape and regularity.
Position within the iris.
Whether the pupils appear constricted or dilated.
Miosis: constricted pupil.
Mydriasis: dilated pupil.
Anisocoria: unequal pupil sizes.
Irregular pupil: may result from previous surgery, trauma, or iris pathology.

A small difference in pupil size can be physiological. Anisocoria that is greater in bright light suggests the larger pupil may be abnormal; anisocoria that is greater in darkness suggests the smaller pupil may be abnormal.

content_groups.group_title: B. Direct and consensual light reflexes

blocks.text: Ask the patient to look at a distant target to reduce accommodation.
Dim the room if possible.
Shine a pen torch into the right eye from the side.
Observe the right pupil for constriction — the direct response.
Observe the left pupil for constriction — the consensual response.
Repeat by illuminating the left eye.

rows: Pupillary constriction when shifting focus to a near target

blocks.text: The afferent limb is carried by the optic nerve (CN II). The signal travels to the pretectal region of the midbrain, with bilateral connections to the Edinger–Westphal nuclei.
The efferent parasympathetic pathway travels with the oculomotor nerve (CN III), synapses in the ciliary ganglion, and reaches the sphincter pupillae through the short ciliary nerves.
Consequently:
Optic nerve damage may impair the afferent light response.
Oculomotor nerve damage may impair constriction of the affected pupil.
Pharmacological agents, iris disease and previous surgery can also affect pupil responses.

content_groups.group_title: D. Swinging flashlight test: relative afferent pupillary defect

blocks.text: This is an essential examination manoeuvre for detecting asymmetric afferent pathway dysfunction.
Ask the patient to fix their gaze on a distant target.
Shine the torch into one eye for approximately 2–3 seconds.
Move the torch rapidly to the other eye.
Continue alternating between the eyes, allowing time for the pupil response to become apparent.
Compare the responses when each eye is illuminated.
Normal response: Both pupils remain constricted when the light is moved between eyes, although a small transient change may occur.
Relative afferent pupillary defect (RAPD): When the light moves from the healthier eye to the affected eye, both pupils appear to dilate or constrict less because the afferent light signal is weaker.
Causes include:
Optic neuritis.
Optic nerve compression or trauma.
Severe asymmetric retinal disease.
Extensive retinal detachment or retinal vascular occlusion.
A RAPD is generally not caused by an uncomplicated cataract alone. Bilateral, symmetrical optic nerve disease may also occur without an RAPD.
Ask the patient to look at a distant object and then shift their gaze to a target held approximately 10–15 cm from the nose.
The normal near response includes:
Convergence of the eyes.
Pupillary constriction.
Accommodation of the lenses.

Clinical significance: A light-near dissociation, in which the pupil responds poorly to light but constricts during near effort, may occur in disorders such as Argyll Robertson pupils and Adie tonic pupil, depending on the clinical context.
This assesses ocular alignment and the function of the extraocular muscles and cranial nerves III, IV and VI.
Before testing movement, look for:
Strabismus or squint.
Abnormal head posture.
Nystagmus.
Ptosis.
Unequal globe position.
Ask the patient to keep their head still and follow your finger with their eyes.
Hold the target at a comfortable distance.
Move it slowly through the six cardinal directions of gaze, forming an H pattern.
Observe both eyes throughout the movement.
Ask whether the patient experiences double vision.
Observe for restricted movement, pain, or nystagmus.
Bring the target towards the nose if you need to assess convergence.
Avoid moving the target excessively far into peripheral gaze, where physiological endpoint nystagmus may occur.

content_groups.group_title: C. Muscles, actions and cranial nerves

rows: Elevation, especially when the eye is abducted
Depression, especially when the eye is abducted
Intorsion; contributes to depression when the eye is adducted
Extorsion; contributes to elevation when the eye is adducted

blocks.text: Mnemonic: LR6, SO4, all the rest 3.
Lateral rectus — sixth cranial nerve.
Superior oblique — fourth cranial nerve.
All remaining extraocular muscles — third cranial nerve.
May produce ptosis, a down-and-out eye, impaired adduction and vertical movements, and sometimes a dilated pupil.
A new third nerve palsy, particularly with pupillary involvement or severe headache, requires emergency assessment because of the possibility of a compressive aneurysm.
May cause vertical or torsional diplopia, especially when reading or descending stairs. Patients may tilt their head to compensate.
Causes impaired abduction of the affected eye and horizontal diplopia, often worse when looking towards the affected side.

Involuntary rhythmic eye movement. Document its direction, whether it is horizontal, vertical or torsional, and whether it occurs in primary or eccentric gaze. New vertical or direction-changing gaze-evoked nystagmus can indicate central neurological pathology.
Important: A normal H-pattern does not exclude every ocular motor disorder. Suspected cranial nerve palsies or complex strabismus may require specialist assessment.

Fundoscopy examines the optic disc, retinal vessels, retina and macula. It is important in patients with visual loss, headache, hypertension, diabetes, neurological symptoms and suspected retinal disease.
Explain that the examination may temporarily dazzle the patient.
Dim the room.
Ask the patient to look at a distant fixed target.
Remove your own spectacles if necessary, while leaving the patient's spectacles on if they are needed and compatible with the examination.
Set the ophthalmoscope to a suitable lens setting and begin with the aperture appropriate to the pupil size.
Examine the patient's right eye with your right eye, holding the ophthalmoscope in your right hand.
Approach from approximately 15 degrees temporal to the patient's line of sight.
Identify the red reflex.
Move closer while keeping the patient's gaze fixed.
Locate the optic disc by following a retinal vessel towards its origin.
Inspect the optic disc and its margins.
Follow the retinal vessels and inspect the background retina.
Ask the patient to look directly at the light briefly to inspect the macula, explaining that this can be uncomfortable.
Repeat on the left eye, using your left eye and left hand.
Assess colour, margins, swelling, cup-to-disc ratio and symmetry.
Normal: pink-orange disc with clearly defined margins.
Pallor: may suggest optic atrophy.
Swollen disc: may indicate papilloedema or other optic disc pathology.
Increased cupping: may occur in glaucoma.
Assess calibre, tortuosity, branching, and arteriovenous crossings.
Hypertensive retinopathy may produce arteriolar narrowing, arteriovenous crossing changes, haemorrhages and cotton-wool spots. Severe hypertension may cause disc swelling.
Look for haemorrhages, exudates, cotton-wool spots, pigment changes, retinal detachment and other abnormalities.
The macula is responsible for central detailed vision. The fovea provides the highest visual acuity.
Macular abnormalities can cause central blur, distortion (metamorphopsia) and central scotomas.
The optic disc contains a central depression called the cup.
The cup-to-disc ratio compares the diameter of the cup with the diameter of the optic disc.
A larger cup may be physiological or associated with glaucoma.
A difference between the two eyes may be significant.
Progressive cupping and thinning of the neuroretinal rim increase suspicion of glaucomatous optic neuropathy.

There is no single cup-to-disc ratio that diagnoses glaucoma in every patient. Interpretation requires the disc size, rim appearance, intraocular pressure, visual fields and, when available, optic nerve imaging.

rows: Raised intracranial pressure, after excluding other causes of disc swelling
Optic atrophy or previous optic nerve injury
Diabetic retinopathy or other retinal vascular disease
Lipid deposition, often associated with vascular leakage
Retinal nerve-fibre layer infarcts; may occur in diabetes, hypertension and other disorders
Retinal vascular disease, trauma, blood disorders and other causes
Pale retina with a cherry-red spot
Central retinal artery occlusion in the appropriate clinical setting

blocks.text: Papilloedema versus optic atrophy: Papilloedema refers to optic disc swelling due to raised intracranial pressure. Optic atrophy refers to loss of optic nerve fibres, often producing disc pallor. Chronic papilloedema may eventually result in optic atrophy.

Direct ophthalmoscopy provides a magnified, upright image but a relatively narrow field of view. It can be difficult to visualise the peripheral retina, and a normal examination does not exclude retinal disease or raised intracranial pressure.
Slit-lamp biomicroscopy, dilated examination and retinal imaging may be required.
Colour vision testing assesses the ability to distinguish colours and can help detect optic nerve dysfunction and inherited colour vision deficiencies.
Ensure adequate, appropriate illumination according to the test instructions.
Hold the plates at the recommended distance.
Test each eye separately, using the patient's usual correction if required.
Ask the patient to identify the number or pattern on each plate.
Present the plates for the specified time.
Record the responses and interpret them according to the test's scoring instructions.
Avoid giving clues or allowing the patient to trace the patterns with their fingers.
Ishihara plates primarily screen for congenital red–green colour vision deficiencies.
Abnormal colour vision can also occur with acquired conditions, particularly optic neuropathies. However, Ishihara testing is not a comprehensive test for all forms of colour vision loss.
Other tests, such as the Farnsworth D-15 or specialised colour arrangement tests, may be used to assess different deficiencies.
Inherited red–green colour deficiency is commonly X-linked.
Acquired colour vision loss may be asymmetric or associated with other visual symptoms.
Reduced colour saturation, especially red desaturation, can be a useful clue to optic nerve dysfunction.
OSCE tip: If one eye perceives a red object as less vivid than the other, document the asymmetry and consider optic nerve disease in the context of visual acuity, pupils and visual fields.
The red reflex is the reddish-orange reflection seen through the pupil when light from an ophthalmoscope reflects from the fundus.
It is particularly important in newborns and children because abnormalities can indicate sight-threatening disease.
Dim the room.
Ask the patient to look straight ahead.
Hold the ophthalmoscope at approximately 30–45 cm from the eyes.
Use the appropriate aperture and illuminate both pupils.
Compare the colour, brightness and symmetry of the reflexes.
If necessary, examine each eye individually at closer range.
Both pupils show a similar red-orange reflex without a focal dark shadow, white reflex or marked asymmetry.
The appearance varies with pigmentation, age, illumination and equipment.
Leukocoria: white pupillary reflex.
Absent or reduced reflex.
Asymmetrical reflexes.
Dark spots or shadows.
Unequal colour or brightness between the eyes.
Possible causes include:
Congenital cataract.
Retinoblastoma.
Corneal opacity.
Vitreous haemorrhage.
Retinal detachment.
Other abnormalities of the ocular media or fundus.

Critical clinical point: A new or persistent white reflex in a child's pupil requires urgent ophthalmic assessment to exclude retinoblastoma and other serious conditions. Do not wait for the next routine appointment.

content_groups.group_title: D. Red reflex versus direct fundoscopy

blocks.text: The red reflex is a screening assessment of the optical pathway through the pupil and ocular media. It is not a substitute for examining the optic disc, vessels, macula and retina.

subsections.subsection_title: Additional important components often examined in OSCEs

blocks.text: Your original list covers the core functional tests, but a comprehensive eye examination should include the following.
Use a pen torch to inspect the cornea and anterior chamber.
Look for:
Corneal opacity, scars or irregularity.
Corneal haze.
Abnormal anterior chamber depth.
Hypopyon (pus-like material layering in the anterior chamber).
Hyphaema (blood in the anterior chamber).
An irregular pupil or suspected iris injury.
A shallow anterior chamber in a patient with a painful red eye, blurred vision, halos and nausea may indicate acute angle-closure glaucoma, which is an emergency.
A pen torch cannot reliably replace slit-lamp assessment of subtle corneal abnormalities or anterior chamber inflammation.
Intraocular pressure (IOP) is the pressure inside the eye.
It may be measured using applanation tonometry, rebound tonometry or other validated devices.
Raised IOP is an important risk factor for glaucoma.
Some patients develop glaucoma despite IOP measurements within the statistically normal range.
A single normal IOP reading does not exclude glaucoma.
A markedly elevated pressure with a painful red eye and reduced vision requires urgent assessment.
Do not measure IOP if an open-globe injury is suspected. Avoid digital pressure on the globe as a substitute for tonometry.
The Amsler grid screens for central visual distortion and scotomas, especially in macular disease.
Ask the patient to wear their usual near-vision correction.
Hold the grid at the recommended reading distance.
Cover one eye.
Ask the patient to look at the central dot without moving their gaze.
Ask whether any lines appear wavy, missing, distorted or blurred.
Repeat with the other eye.
A new distortion or central scotoma requires prompt assessment, particularly if associated with sudden symptoms.
Ask the patient to look at a pen torch held directly in front of them. Observe where the light is reflected from each cornea.
The reflections should be approximately symmetrical in a normally aligned gaze. Asymmetry can suggest ocular misalignment.
This helps identify a manifest deviation (tropia).
Ask the patient to fixate on a target.
Cover one eye and observe the uncovered eye.
Remove the cover and watch for refixation movements.
Repeat on the other side.
A refixation movement of the uncovered eye suggests a manifest deviation.
When clinically indicated, assess corneal sensation with a fine wisp of cotton, approaching from the side to avoid triggering a visual response. Compare the two eyes.
Corneal sensation is mediated by the ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve (CN V1). Reduced sensation can occur with herpetic disease, trigeminal dysfunction and other corneal disorders.
Do not touch the cornea with an instrument during a routine screening examination unless the test is indicated and performed appropriately.

content_groups.group_title: G. Eyelid closure and lacrimal function

blocks.text: Assess whether the patient can close the eyelids fully. Incomplete closure may lead to exposure keratopathy.
Inspect for excessive tearing, dry-eye symptoms and lacrimal sac swelling. Additional tear-film testing may be required when dry eye is suspected.
Children require age-appropriate testing:
Infants: fixation, following, preferential looking or age-appropriate objective assessment.
Preschool children: picture or symbol charts, such as LEA symbols or HOTV.
Older children: Snellen or logMAR charts, depending on their ability.

A child who cannot cooperate with a standard chart should not automatically be recorded as having normal vision. Assess fixation, alignment, red reflexes and other age-appropriate indicators, and arrange formal assessment when indicated.

subsections.subsection_title: How to integrate the findings clinically

blocks.text: The most useful approach is to interpret multiple examination components together rather than in isolation.

rows: Marked acuity reduction, RAPD may be present
Retinal artery occlusion, retinal detachment, optic nerve ischaemia
Painful red eye with blurred vision
Corneal haze, abnormal pupil, possible raised IOP
Abnormal Amsler grid, possible macular changes
Misalignment, restricted movement, abnormal ocular motor examination
Cranial nerve palsy, extraocular muscle disorder, neuromuscular disease
Headache with transient visual obscurations or disc swelling
Raised intracranial pressure; urgent evaluation required
Cataract, retinoblastoma and other ocular pathology

blocks.text: These are clinical associations, not definitive diagnoses. Sudden visual loss, a suspected retinal artery occlusion or detachment, a painful red eye with visual reduction, new neurological deficits, or suspected papilloedema warrants urgent evaluation.
Testing both eyes together and missing unilateral impairment.
Forgetting to document whether the patient wore corrective lenses.
Failing to perform pinhole testing when acuity is reduced.
Comparing visual fields without maintaining fixation.
Missing a relative afferent pupillary defect.
Moving the patient's head instead of testing eye movements.
Forgetting to ask about diplopia during extraocular movement testing.
Failing to assess the optic disc margins during fundoscopy.
Assuming a normal red reflex excludes all retinal pathology.
Diagnosing glaucoma from the cup-to-disc ratio or IOP alone.
Omitting urgent referral when serious warning signs are present.

subsections.subsection_title: How to present your findings to the examiner

blocks.text: Use a concise, systematic presentation that includes the positive and negative findings relevant to the clinical situation.
Visual acuity was 6/6 in each eye with the patient's usual correction. Visual fields were full to confrontation bilaterally.

The eyes were symmetrical, with no proptosis, ptosis, conjunctival injection or obvious corneal opacity. The pupils were equal and regular, with brisk direct and consensual light reflexes and no relative afferent pupillary defect.
Extraocular movements were full, with no diplopia or pathological nystagmus. Colour vision was intact on the screening test performed.
The red reflexes were present and symmetrical bilaterally. Fundoscopy showed pink optic discs with distinct margins, no obvious disc swelling, and no significant retinal haemorrhages or exudates.
There was no obvious abnormality on the components of the eye examination performed.
Only report findings that you actually assessed. If you did not perform fundoscopy, tonometry or formal visual field testing, state that rather than claiming a normal result.

items: Introduce yourself, obtain consent and ask about symptoms
Inspect facial symmetry, orbits and eyelids
Measure distance visual acuity in each eye
Perform pinhole testing if acuity is reduced
Assess pupil size, shape and direct/consensual responses
Assess the near response when indicated
Test extraocular movements in an H pattern

blocks.text: Assess the anterior chamber and intraocular pressure when indicated and safe

items: Perform Amsler grid or other targeted tests when indicated
Thank the patient, explain findings and arrange appropriate follow-up

blocks.text: Visual acuity assesses central resolving power.
Visual fields help localise visual pathway lesions.
CN II is the afferent limb of the pupillary light reflex; CN III carries the parasympathetic efferent limb.
LR6, SO4, all the rest 3.
RAPD suggests asymmetric afferent pathway dysfunction.
Optic disc swelling, pallor and cupping have different clinical meanings.
The red reflex is particularly important in paediatric examinations.
A normal screening examination does not exclude all eye disease.
The goal is to combine the examination findings into a coherent clinical interpretation, recognise sight-threatening conditions early, and know when specialist ophthalmic assessment is necessary.

subsections.subsection_title: How to present a normal eye examination

blocks.text: A systematic eye examination includes visual function, external inspection, pupils, ocular movements, visual fields and fundoscopy.
You can use this model when the examination is entirely normal.

"On examination, the patient is comfortable and has no obvious facial asymmetry or periorbital abnormality. Visual acuity is normal in both eyes, with and without correction as appropriate. Visual fields are full to confrontation. The pupils are equal, round and reactive to light, with normal direct and consensual light reflexes and no relative afferent pupillary defect.

Extraocular movements are full and painless in all directions, with no diplopia or nystagmus. The conjunctivae are pink, the sclerae are white, and the corneas are clear. The anterior chambers appear normal, and there is no obvious abnormality of the iris or lens on examination.

On fundoscopy, the optic discs have distinct margins, the cup-to-disc ratios are within the expected range, the retinal vessels are normal, and there are no retinal haemorrhages, exudates or other visible abnormalities."
Important: Only report findings you actually examined. Direct ophthalmoscopy cannot reliably establish that every part of the anterior chamber, lens or retina is normal.

subsections.subsection_title: B. The systematic examination and what to report

rows: Normal and comparable in both eyes, with correction documented
Full to confrontation in all tested quadrants
No ptosis, proptosis, swelling, discharge or facial asymmetry
Conjunctiva pink; sclera white; no injection or jaundice
Equal, round and reactive to light; no RAPD
Full and painless in all directions
No manifest squint; corneal light reflexes symmetrical
Disc margins distinct; vessels and visible retina without obvious abnormalities
Present and symmetrical in both eyes

blocks.text: The examiner wants more than a description. You should state the abnormality, its clinical significance and, where appropriate, your likely differential diagnosis.
Report: "Visual acuity is reduced in the right eye to 6/24, compared with 6/6 in the left eye, using the patient's usual correction."
Possible causes: Refractive error, cataract, corneal opacity, macular disease, optic neuropathy or retinal disease.
Next step: Test pinhole acuity. Improvement suggests a refractive component, although it does not exclude coexisting disease.

items: 2. Reduced acuity that improves with pinhole

blocks.text: Report: "Visual acuity improves from 6/24 to 6/9 with pinhole, suggesting a significant refractive component."
Interpretation: Uncorrected refractive error is likely. Improvement is not proof that the eye is otherwise healthy.
6/6: Standard distance visual acuity.
6/12: At 6 metres, the patient reads what a person with standard acuity can read at 12 metres.
6/60: Markedly reduced distance visual acuity.
CF: Counting fingers, when the patient cannot read the chart's largest letters.
HM: Hand movements.
PL: Perception of light.
NPL: No perception of light.
Document the testing distance, each eye separately, and whether correction or pinhole was used.

rows: "The pupils are unequal in diameter, measuring 5 mm on the right and 3 mm on the left."
Compare in bright and dim light; consider physiological anisocoria, Horner syndrome or third-nerve palsy
"The right pupil is dilated and poorly reactive to light."
Consider pharmacological causes, iris trauma, acute third-nerve palsy and acute angle-closure glaucoma in the appropriate context
Consider Horner syndrome, opioids or uveitis, depending on associated findings
"A relative afferent pupillary defect is present in the right eye."
Suggests asymmetric retinal or optic nerve dysfunction
May occur with previous ocular surgery, trauma or posterior synechiae from uveitis

blocks.text: Emergency distinction: A new dilated pupil with ptosis, diplopia or restricted eye movements may indicate a compressive third-nerve palsy. A painful red eye with blurred vision, halos, headache, nausea and a poorly reactive mid-dilated pupil raises concern for acute angle-closure glaucoma. Both require urgent assessment.

rows: Right sixth cranial nerve palsy or mechanical restriction
Third nerve dysfunction, internuclear ophthalmoplegia or mechanical restriction
Ptosis with eye down and out
"Left ptosis with a down-and-out resting position and impaired adduction, elevation and depression."
"The patient reports double vision on right gaze, corresponding to restricted right abduction."
Possible sixth nerve palsy; establish whether diplopia is binocular or monocular
"There is horizontal jerk nystagmus on right gaze."
May be vestibular, neurological, medication-related or physiological at extreme gaze

blocks.text: Clinical pearl: New ocular movement abnormalities accompanied by severe headache, unequal pupils, focal neurological signs or acute visual loss warrant urgent evaluation.

subsections.subsection_title: D. Red eye and anterior segment abnormalities

rows: "There is diffuse conjunctival redness with watery discharge."
Viral conjunctivitis, allergic conjunctivitis or other conjunctival inflammation
"There is conjunctival injection with mucopurulent discharge."
"There is circumcorneal injection, most prominent around the limbus."
Anterior uveitis or acute angle-closure glaucoma
"The cornea is not completely transparent, with a focal opacity."
"There is a focal corneal epithelial defect with an underlying stromal infiltrate."
Microbial keratitis; urgent ophthalmic assessment is required
"A visible layer of inflammatory cells is present in the anterior chamber."
"Blood is visible in the anterior chamber."
Usually trauma; assess urgently for associated ocular injury
"There is lens opacity with a reduced red reflex."
Thyroid eye disease, orbital inflammation, tumour or haemorrhage

blocks.text: Conjunctivitis: Irritation, discharge and diffuse redness; vision is usually preserved.
Anterior uveitis: Pain, photophobia, ciliary flush and sometimes a small or irregular pupil.
Acute angle-closure glaucoma: Severe pain, reduced vision, halos, headache, nausea, a hazy cornea and a mid-dilated poorly reactive pupil.
Keratitis/corneal ulcer: Pain, photophobia, reduced vision and possible corneal opacity or fluorescein staining.
Do not label a painful red eye as simple conjunctivitis without checking visual acuity and assessing for corneal or intraocular disease.

rows: "The optic discs are swollen bilaterally with blurred margins."
Suggests raised intracranial pressure in the appropriate context; urgent assessment is required
"The optic disc appears pale compared with the surrounding retina."
Previous or ongoing optic nerve damage
"The cup-to-disc ratio is increased, with possible neuroretinal rim thinning."
Suggests glaucoma; correlate with intraocular pressure, visual fields and OCT
"There are retinal microaneurysms and dot-blot haemorrhages, with or without exudates or neovascularisation."
"There is arteriolar narrowing with arteriovenous crossing changes and/or retinal haemorrhages."
"There is an elevated, folded or corrugated retinal appearance."
Suspected retinal detachment; urgent ophthalmology referral
"There is an abnormal appearance of the macular region."
Could reflect macular degeneration, oedema or other macular disease

blocks.text: Papilloedema is specifically optic disc swelling associated with raised intracranial pressure, not a synonym for every swollen disc.
A normal-looking fundus does not exclude optic neuritis, early glaucoma or other serious causes of visual loss.
Acute flashes, new floaters or a curtain-like shadow over the vision may indicate retinal tear or detachment, even before the patient notices severe visual loss.
These are classic OSCE distinctions that commonly appear in viva questions.

subsections.subsection_title: Optic nerve versus ocular motor nerve lesions

rows: Reduced visual acuity or field defect; RAPD may be present in asymmetric disease.
Ptosis, impaired adduction/elevation/depression; pupil may be dilated in compressive lesions.
Vertical or torsional diplopia, often worse when looking down, e.g. descending stairs.
Impaired abduction and horizontal diplopia worse on gaze toward the affected side.

items: Anisocoria is often greater in darkness
Eye may rest down and out
Pupil may be dilated if parasympathetic fibres are involved

blocks.text: Neither pupil involvement nor its absence alone reliably determines whether a third-nerve palsy is an aneurysm. A new suspected palsy requires urgent assessment.
RAPD: An abnormal relative response when light is alternated between the eyes; suggests asymmetric afferent pathway dysfunction.
Fixed pupil: A pupil that fails to constrict appropriately; possible causes include pharmacological dilation, iris damage, severe ocular disease or efferent nerve dysfunction.
An RAPD can occur despite pupils appearing equal in size.
Swollen optic disc, blurred margins and possible venous congestion. Central visual acuity may initially be preserved.
Pale disc due to optic nerve fibre loss; visual acuity, colour vision or visual fields may be impaired.

subsections.subsection_title: Common OSCE "Why did you do that?" questions

blocks.text: The examiner is testing whether you understand the clinical purpose of each manoeuvre.

rows: Why do you examine visual acuity first?
It establishes baseline visual function and identifies potentially urgent visual impairment.
To detect unilateral or asymmetric disease that binocular viewing may conceal.
It reduces peripheral light rays and helps identify a refractive component to reduced acuity.
To detect defects due to retinal, optic nerve, chiasmal, optic tract or more posterior visual pathway lesions.
Why check pupils before dilating them?
Dilation can interfere with assessment of pupil size and light responses.
To detect a relative afferent pupillary defect, suggesting asymmetric optic nerve or severe retinal dysfunction.
Why test direct and consensual light reflexes?
To assess the afferent and efferent pathways of the pupillary light reflex.
Why assess ocular movements in six directions?
To evaluate extraocular muscle function and the third, fourth and sixth cranial nerves.
It may reveal ocular misalignment or cranial nerve dysfunction not obvious on inspection.
To assess near-response function and the ability of both eyes to converge on a near target.
Why inspect the cornea with a light?
To identify opacity, surface irregularity, injury or infection.
To detect media opacity or asymmetry, including cataract and some intraocular abnormalities.
To inspect the optic disc, retinal vessels, retina and macula where visible.
Why inspect the optic disc margins?
Blurring or swelling may indicate optic disc pathology, including papilloedema.
Acquired colour desaturation, especially red desaturation, may suggest optic nerve dysfunction.
It can indicate third-nerve palsy, Horner syndrome, myasthenia gravis or local eyelid disease.
Why ask about contact lens use?
Contact lens wear increases the risk of microbial keratitis, including potentially sight-threatening infection.
Why check visual acuity in a patient with a red eye?
Reduced acuity is a red flag for corneal, intraocular or other sight-threatening pathology.
To assess for raised pressure; pressure alone neither confirms nor excludes glaucoma.
Why examine the eye movements in a patient with proptosis?
Restriction may indicate orbital involvement, inflammation or mechanical impairment.

blocks.text: Visual acuity, visual fields and colour vision.
Size, shape, direct and consensual reflexes, RAPD.
Eyelids, conjunctiva, sclera, cornea, anterior segment and alignment.
Ocular motility, diplopia and nystagmus.
Red reflex, optic disc, vessels, retina and macula.
This is a revision mnemonic, not a mandatory examination order. Visual acuity should be checked early, and the exact sequence may vary with the station.

subsections.subsection_title: B. Causes of a red eye: "C-U-K-G"

blocks.text: C — Conjunctivitis: Discharge, irritation, diffuse injection.
U — Uveitis: Pain, photophobia, ciliary flush.
K — Keratitis: Pain, photophobia, corneal lesion.
G — Glaucoma (acute angle closure): Pain, blurred vision, halos, headache, nausea and a poorly reactive mid-dilated pupil.
This mnemonic covers important differentials, not every cause of red eye. Scleritis, trauma and endophthalmitis are additional serious possibilities.

subsections.subsection_title: C. Causes of a white pupil or absent red reflex: "C-R-R-V"

items: V — Persistent fetal vasculature (formerly persistent hyperplastic primary vitreous)

blocks.text: A white pupil (leukocoria), particularly in a child, requires urgent ophthalmic assessment. Retinoblastoma must be excluded.

subsections.subsection_title: D. Cranial nerves controlling eye movement: "LR6 SO4, the rest 3"

items: All other extraocular muscles — CN III

blocks.text: The pupillary reflex depends on an intact afferent pathway (CN II) and efferent parasympathetic pathway (CN III).

When light is moved from a normal eye to an eye with an afferent defect, both pupils may appear to dilate relative to their previous constriction. This is the classic swinging-flashlight finding in RAPD.

subsections.subsection_title: F. Visual pathway: "Nasal fibres Navigate across"

blocks.text: Nasal retinal fibres cross at the optic chiasm.
Temporal retinal fibres remain on the same side.
Chiasmal lesions classically produce bitemporal visual field loss.
Optic tract or more posterior lesions often cause contralateral homonymous field defects.

subsections.subsection_title: How to present common abnormal cases to an examiner

blocks.text: These concise presentations help you move from examination findings to a clinical impression.

"Visual acuity is reduced in the affected eye, with red desaturation and a relative afferent pupillary defect. The anterior segment is unremarkable. The optic disc may be normal or swollen. These findings suggest an optic neuropathy, with optic neuritis among the differentials."

"The affected eye is red and painful, with reduced visual acuity, a hazy cornea and a mid-dilated poorly reactive pupil. The findings are concerning for acute angle-closure glaucoma. I would arrange immediate ophthalmology assessment and avoid delaying treatment for routine investigations."

"There is ptosis, an abnormal resting eye position and impaired adduction, elevation and depression. These findings suggest an oculomotor nerve palsy. I would urgently assess the pupil, onset, headache and associated neurological signs, and arrange emergency investigation for a compressive cause when indicated."

"Fundoscopy reveals retinal microaneurysms and haemorrhages, with or without hard exudates, cotton-wool spots or neovascularisation. These findings are compatible with diabetic retinopathy. I would document severity and macular involvement and arrange appropriate retinal assessment."

"Both optic discs appear swollen with blurred margins. This raises concern for papilloedema in the appropriate clinical context. I would assess for headache, vomiting, transient visual obscurations and neurological signs, and arrange urgent evaluation for raised intracranial pressure. I would not perform a lumbar puncture until a mass lesion and other contraindications have been appropriately assessed."
Use this as a rapid revision checklist before entering the examination station.
Introduce yourself, confirm identity, obtain consent and wash hands.
Check visual acuity in each eye separately, with correction and pinhole where appropriate.
Assess visual fields and colour vision when indicated.
Inspect eyelids, lashes, conjunctivae, sclerae, corneas and ocular alignment.
Assess pupil size, shape, direct and consensual responses, and RAPD.
Examine ocular movements, diplopia and nystagmus.
Assess the red reflex and perform fundoscopy where indicated.
Check intraocular pressure when indicated and safe; avoid tonometry if open-globe injury is suspected.
Summarise positive and relevant negative findings and state your clinical impression.
Recognise sight-threatening abnormalities and arrange urgent escalation.

Examiner's golden rule: State the finding, localise the likely problem, give the leading differential and mention the next appropriate action. In ophthalmology, sudden visual loss, a painful red eye with reduced vision, suspected retinal detachment and a new pupil-involving third-nerve palsy must never be treated as routine OSCE findings.
